# Performance

BPL interprets each function call once, then runs it on the whole array in compiled Rust. Interpreting a call costs about the same whatever the size of its arguments. On large arrays, the time goes into the data. BPL also runs chains of calls on large arrays together, in one pass over memory, and compiles that pass into machine code. Static kinds let more calls take these routes.

## Static kinds

Dynamic kinds, the default, suit interactive analysis. Integers are exact and never wrap, and some results take their kind from their values, as `√¯4` gives a complex number. Static kinds, which `•prefs ["kinds":"static"]` sets, are the setting for performance work. Each result's kind follows from its arguments' kinds. BPL then knows the type of every result before a computation runs. More calls can run together. Under dynamic kinds, `⌊` gives exact integers and runs on its own. Under static kinds, it gives floats and runs with the multiplication and the sum:

```bpl
y←¿200000⍴0
(•explain "+/⌊10×y").fused.glyphs      ⍝ 0⍴⊂""
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
(•explain "+/⌊10×y").fused.glyphs      ⍝ ["×⌊+/"]
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
```

Code meant for static kinds gives each integer the width that its values need and gives `•csv` and `•json` a `types` record for their columns. [Numbers](numbers.qmd#static-kinds) shows how code written for dynamic kinds can give other results under static kinds.

## Calls that wait

An elementwise call on 131,072 numbers or more doesn't compute at once. It waits, and the calls that read its result join it. When something needs the items, the whole chain runs together, block by block. It reads each input array once and writes only what it must keep. A chain of arithmetic that ends in a reduction runs in about the time that one copy of its data takes. [`•explain`](system/explain.qmd) lists the calls of each group that ran together:

```bpl
y←¿1000000⍴0
(•explain "+/ 2×y+1.5 - 1").fused.glyphs    ⍝ ["+×-+/"]
```

Waiting costs a fixed amount of planning on each call. It pays only on large arrays.

Structural functions such as `⌽`, `⍉`, `↑`, `↓` and `↕` wait too, on large arrays of any kind. They hold only where each item of their result comes from. Such a view stays a view until a call needs its items in memory. Calls that run together read through it without building it:

```bpl
w←1000↕¿1000000⍴0
(•storage w).pending     ⍝ $t
```

[`•prefs`](system/prefs.qmd) lists the glyphs whose calls run together, under `fusion`. Any other call, such as `⍋`, computes the waiting items it reads first. So does display. The `fusion` setting writes a line where each group ends. A waiting call keeps the settings in force when it was called.

## Compiled loops

A group of 3,145,728 items or more compiles its loop into machine code. The compiled loop keeps intermediate values in registers. A smaller group compiles too where the process has already compiled its loop. A compile takes about a millisecond. `•explain` records whether each group compiled:

```bpl
y←¿3145728⍴0
(•explain "+/ 2×y+1.5 - 1").fused.compiled    ⍝ [$t]
```

The browser build compiles nothing at run time. Its groups run on kernels built into the module, as [BPL on the web](web.ipynb#differences-from-native-bpl) describes.

## Maps

Each, Rank, stencils and outer products call a dfn once, on all their cells together, where they can. `{⍵×⍵+1}¨v` then costs about what `v×v+1` costs. [Evaluation](evaluation.qmd#functions-and-effects) gives the rules. With the `batch` setting at `$f`, a map calls its operand once for each cell.

## The cost of a call

Each call pays a fixed cost to interpret it, whatever the size of its arguments. A call of `{⍵}` costs about 1,500 machine instructions. Each call of a recursive Fibonacci function costs about 4,600. A loop over the items of a million-item array pays that cost a million times. Code that works on whole arrays pays it once for each call. Compiling doesn't remove this cost. Only the loops inside a group compile.

## Names and writes

A dfn releases each local name after the last statement that reads it. A waiting computation that only the name held then runs with the calls that read it. In `f`, the arithmetic and the sum run as one group, and nothing is stored on the way:

```bpl
big←¿1000000⍴0
f←{a←⍵×2 ⋄ b←a+1 ⋄ +/a×b}
(•explain "f big").fused.glyphs       ⍝ ["×+×+/"]
≢(•explain "f big").stored.glyphs     ⍝ 0ₓ
```

[Dfns](dfns.ipynb#scope) describes what a released name means for `⍎`.

A write to part of an array that nothing else holds changes the array in place. `x,←v` and `x⍪←v` add to the end of the array's storage. `x←x,v` copies the whole array, because `x` still holds the old array while `x,v` is computed. [Assignment](assignment.ipynb) describes each form of write.

## Threads

Large calls split across the machine's cores. A call splits only when it has enough work to repay the extra threads. The `threads` setting sets how many threads a call can use. Several BPL processes running at once compete for the cores unless each sets `threads` to 1. The browser build runs every call on one thread.

## Seeing what happened

[`•explain`](system/explain.qmd) runs code and records each route it took: groups that ran together, compiles, calls that computed waiting items, and maps that fell back to a call for each cell. [`•memory`](system/memory.qmd) counts the waiting arrays and other values that a thread holds, and the bytes that a value keeps alive. [`•storage`](system/storage.qmd) shows how an array is held, and whether it's still waiting.

## Derivatives

[`∂`](glyphs/partial.qmd) traces the function it differentiates into a program of typed steps. The program runs through the same groups and compiled loops. Later calls replay it while their arguments and free names still fit it. Under dynamic kinds, a call whose result type can depend on its values stops a trace. On reals, those calls are `√` and every root but the cube root `3√`, `⍟`, `!`, `0○`, and `*` whose exponent isn't a whole number or is the value being differentiated. `∂` then runs without a program:

```bpl
(•explain "{+/√⍵}∂1 2 3").programs.event      ⍝ 0⍴⊂""
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
(•explain "{+/√⍵}∂1 2 3").programs.event      ⍝ ["built"]
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
```

[Automatic differentiation](autodiff.qmd) describes how `∂` works.

## Not built yet

The plan includes:

- One pass for several reductions of the same data. Today each reduction, as in `+/v ÷ ⌈/v`, makes its own pass.
- A tracing point for whole training steps, such as `⍣`. A repeated step's forward pass, gradient and update would then run as one program.
- Programs for maps whose cells take different branches, so that `∂` can trace them.
- The GPU, through WebGPU, with 16-bit brain floats (bf16), and compiled code in the browser.
